function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

I’m happy to help you get started with a “startup‑stat” API—but first I just need a little more context so I can point you at the right resource: | Question | Why it matters | |----------|----------------| | **What kind of startup data do you need?**
• Funding & valuation
• Employee size & growth
• Revenue & profitability
• Product roadmap & tech stack
• Market traction (users, ARR, churn)
• Competitive landscape | Different providers expose different fields – knowing what you care about narrows down the best source. | | **Do you already have access to a paid database?**
(Crunchbase Pro, PitchBook, CB Insights, Dealroom, etc.) | Some APIs require a subscription; others offer free tiers. | | **Will this be used internally only, or exposed publicly?** | Public exposure may trigger stricter rate limits or licensing constraints. | | **How many startups / queries per day/month?** | Rate limiting varies widely between vendors. | --- ### Quick Overview of Popular Startup‑Data APIs Below is a snapshot of the most common APIs you’ll encounter when pulling startup statistics. For each provider I list: * Typical use case * Authentication method * Key endpoints (with example URLs) * Rough pricing/rate‑limit notes Feel free to pick whichever matches your needs—or let me know if none fit and we can brainstorm alternatives! | Provider | Use Case | Auth | Sample Endpoints | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Crunchbase Data API v3** | Comprehensive company profiles + funding history | OAuth 2.0 bearer token (API key) | `GET https://api.crunchbase.com/v3.1/organizations/`
`GET https://api.crunchbase.com/v3.1/funding_rounds?q=organization:&page=` | Free tier limited to ~200 req/day; paid plans start ~$99/mo. | | **AngelList API** | Early‑stage companies, job listings, investor networks | Basic Auth (client ID+secret) | `GET https://angel.co/api/startups.json?page=

&per_page=` | No official docs—community maintained wrappers available. | | **PitchBook API** (via Bloomberg Terminal) | Private equity & VC deals, detailed financials | Enterprise login | `/companies`, `/deals` | Very expensive (~$10k+/yr). | | **Dealroom.io API** | European market focus, M&A activity | Bearer token | `https://api.dealroom.eu/v1/company//overview` | Paid plans $50–$500/mo depending on volume. | | **SeedInvest API** | Crowdfunding round data | JWT | `GET https://api.seedinvest.com/v1/crowdfunds/` | Limited public documentation. | | **OpenCorporates API** | Company registration records worldwide | API key | `GET https://api.opencorporates.com/v0.4/companies/search?q=` | Freemium; higher rates cost money. | | **GitHub REST API** (for open‑source projects) | Repo stars, forks, contributors | Personal Access Token | `GET https://api.github.com/repos/:owner/:repo/stats/contributors` | Useful for measuring product maturity indirectly. | --- #### Example Request Using `requests` ```python import requests BASE_URL = "https://api.crunchbase.com/v3.1" def fetch_company(org_slug): url = f"{BASE_URL}/organizations/{org_slug}" params = {"user_key": ""} resp = requests.get(url, params=params) return resp.json() company_data = fetch_company("stripe") print(company_data["data"]["properties"]) ``` Replace `` with your actual key. Most other providers follow similar patterns (`Bearer ` in the Authorization header). --- ### Building Your Own Internal Stats Endpoint If you’re aggregating multiple sources into a single unified view, consider exposing something like: ``` POST /internal-api/startup-stats # Ingest raw data from various feeds GET /internal-api/startups/{uuid}/stats # Return consolidated JSON DELETE /internal-api/startups/{uuid} # Remove stale entries ``` Typical payload structure: ```json { "uuid": "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000", "name": "Acme Corp", "funding_total_usd": 125_000_000, "employees_current": 250, "revenue_last_year_usd": 45_000_000, "product_stage": "Series B", "market_segment": ["FinTech", "SaaS"], "last_updated_at": "2026-04-30T14:22Z" } ``` Use caching layers (Redis/LRU), pagination, and proper error handling to keep latency low. --- ### Next Steps 1. **Clarify Requirements:** Let me know which data points matter most to you and whether you already have vendor access. 2. **Choose Vendor(s):** Pick one or combine several based on coverage vs. cost. 3. **Set Up Credentials:** Register for an API key/token. 4. **Prototype Calls:** Test against sandbox environments where possible. 5. **Integrate & Cache:** Build wrapper modules around the chosen API(s); add local cache to reduce quota hits. Once you confirm the specifics, I can dive deeper into exact endpoint paths, parameter lists, pagination strategies, and even generate ready‑to‑copy client libraries in Python, JavaScript, or Go!
